blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 5 (Enzymes), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Enzymes are also known as:
blocks.explanation: Enzymes are specific proteins that speed up reactions without being altered; they are also called biocatalysts (5.1).

book_ref.quote: Enzymes are also known as biocatalysts

blocks.prompt: 2 Rates of enzyme-catalysed reactions may be greater than those of uncatalysed reactions by:
blocks.explanation: Rates of enzyme-catalysed reactions may be 10³ to 10⁸ times greater than the uncatalysed reactions (5.1).

book_ref.quote: Rates of enzyme-catalysed reactions may be 10³ to 10⁸ times greater

blocks.prompt: 3 All enzymes are synthesized inside cells by:
blocks.explanation: All enzymes are synthesized inside cells by ribosomes; then they work inside the cell or are secreted out (5.1).

book_ref.quote: All enzymes are synthesized inside cells by ribosomes

blocks.prompt: 4 The enzymes of glycolysis are found:
blocks.explanation: Many enzymes, such as those of glycolysis, are dissolved in the cytoplasm (5.1).

book_ref.quote: Inside cell, many enzymes are dissolved in cytoplasm; for example, the enzymes of glycolysis

blocks.prompt: 5 The enzymes of protein synthesis are:
blocks.explanation: Some enzymes, e.g. those of protein synthesis, are an integral part of ribosomes (5.1).

book_ref.quote: Some enzymes are integral part of ribosomes; for example, the enzymes of protein synthesis

blocks.prompt: 6 A reaction completed in 30 minutes with an enzyme would take, without the enzyme, about:
blocks.explanation: A reaction completed in 30 minutes with an enzyme would take one year without it (5.1).

book_ref.quote: would take one year to get completed without being catalysed by enzyme

blocks.prompt: 7 The reactions in red blood cells differ from those in nerve cells because these cells:

options.text: have the same enzymes at different pH
use enzymes only outside the cell

blocks.explanation: All cells do not have the same set of enzymes; red blood cells and nerve cells contain different sets (5.1).

book_ref.quote: red blood cells and nerve cells contain different sets of enzymes

blocks.prompt: 8 The small cleft on the surface of an enzyme, made of a few amino acids, where catalysis occurs, is the:
blocks.explanation: The active site is a small cleft of only a few amino acids on the globular enzyme; catalysis occurs there (Active Site).

book_ref.quote: This site is known as active site

blocks.prompt: 9 The substrate fits into the binding site of the active site by:

options.text: weak chemical forces such as hydrogen bonds

blocks.explanation: The substrate fits into the binding site by weak chemical forces such as hydrogen bonds; the catalytic site then catalyses the reaction (Active Site).

book_ref.quote: Substrate molecule fits into binding site by weak chemical forces

blocks.prompt: 10 The two distinct regions of an active site are:
blocks.explanation: The active site has a binding site (holds the substrate) and a catalytic site (transforms it into products) (Active Site).

book_ref.quote: Active site has two distinct regions i.e., binding site and catalytic site

blocks.prompt: 11 Pepsin is produced in an inactive form called:
blocks.explanation: Pepsin could destroy protein structures in the cells that make it, so it is produced as inactive pepsinogen and activated at its target site (Active Site).

book_ref.quote: That is why it is produced in inactive form (pepsinogen)

blocks.prompt: 12 Chemically, enzymes are:
blocks.explanation: Enzymes are three-dimensional globular proteins of polypeptide chains coiled upon themselves (Active Site).

book_ref.quote: Enzymes are three-dimensional globular proteins

blocks.prompt: 13 How many kinds of cofactors are described?
blocks.explanation: There are three kinds of cofactor: metal ions, prosthetic groups and coenzymes (5.2).

book_ref.quote: There are three kinds of cofactor: metal ions, prosthetic groups, and coenzymes

blocks.prompt: 14 The protein part of an enzyme is called the:
blocks.explanation: The protein part is the apoenzyme; the complete enzyme including cofactor is the holoenzyme (5.2).

book_ref.quote: The protein part of enzyme is called apoenzyme

blocks.prompt: 15 Apoenzyme + cofactor =
blocks.explanation: The complete enzyme including its cofactor is called the holoenzyme (5.2).

book_ref.quote: complete enzyme including co-factor is called holoenzyme

blocks.prompt: 16 Metal ion cofactors act by:

options.text: changing non-functional active sites into functional sites
forming covalent bonds with the substrate

blocks.explanation: Metal ions change non-functional active sites into functional ones; the attachment also changes the enzyme's shape so it can combine with substrate (5.2).

book_ref.quote: These metal ions change the non-functional active sites of enzymes into functional sites

blocks.prompt: 17 Hematin is an example of a:
blocks.explanation: Cofactors forming covalent bonds with the enzyme are prosthetic groups; one organic example is hematin (5.2).

book_ref.quote: Some cofactors form covalent bonds with enzyme and are known as prosthetic groups

blocks.prompt: 18 Which vitamins are named as functioning as coenzymes?
blocks.explanation: Many vitamins, e.g. niacin and riboflavin, function as coenzymes; some are parts of coenzymes (5.2).

book_ref.quote: Many vitamins (e.g., niacin and riboflavin) function as coenzymes

blocks.prompt: 19 When NAD⁺ acquires a hydrogen atom, it is reduced to:
blocks.explanation: NAD⁺, the most important coenzyme, is a hydrogen acceptor; on acquiring a hydrogen atom it reduces to NADH, which carries the energy of the electron (5.2).

book_ref.quote: When NAD⁺ acquires a hydrogen atom from an enzyme, it reduces to NADH

blocks.prompt: 20 A non-protein organic cofactor loosely attached to the enzyme is a:
blocks.explanation: A loosely attached non-protein organic cofactor is a coenzyme; a covalently bonded one is a prosthetic group (5.2).

book_ref.quote: When the cofactor is a non-protein organic molecule and is loosely attached with enzyme

blocks.prompt: 21 Trace elements used by enzymes as cofactors include:
blocks.explanation: Trace elements such as molybdenum and manganese, necessary for health, are used by enzymes as cofactors (5.2).

book_ref.quote: Many trace elements such as molybdenum and manganese

blocks.prompt: 22 The speed of a chemical reaction depends on the amount of:

options.text: activation energy required to start it

blocks.explanation: The speed of a reaction depends on the activation energy needed to initiate it; enzymes lower it (5.3).

book_ref.quote: Activation energy is the energy which works to destabilize existing chemical bonds

blocks.prompt: 23 The presence of an enzyme affects a reaction by:

options.text: being used up in the reaction

blocks.explanation: Enzymes do not affect the nature or properties of end products: sucrose always gives glucose and fructose, with or without sucrase (5.3).

book_ref.quote: sucrose (substrate) will always be hydrolysed into glucose and fructose

blocks.prompt: 24 When the substrate binds with the active site, the structure formed is the:
blocks.explanation: The substrate binds the active site forming an ES complex, and the catalytic site is activated (5.3).

book_ref.quote: an enzyme-substrate complex (ES complex) is formed and catalytic site is activated

blocks.prompt: 25 After the products are formed, the enzyme:

options.text: detaches unaltered and can act again

blocks.explanation: After the reaction the enzyme detaches from the products in an unaltered state: E + S → ES → E + P (5.3).

book_ref.quote: enzyme detaches itself from the products, in an unaltered state

blocks.prompt: 26 In a metabolic pathway, the product of one enzyme's catalysis:

options.text: serves as substrate for the next enzyme

blocks.explanation: In pathways such as respiration and photosynthesis, enzymes act in sequence; the product of one serves as substrate for the next (5.3).

book_ref.quote: The successive enzymes controlling these steps are present together along with their cofactors

blocks.prompt: 27 The lock-and-key model was proposed in 1894 by:
blocks.explanation: The German chemist Emil Fischer proposed the lock-and-key model in 1894 (Models).

book_ref.quote: In 1894 a German chemist Emil Fischer proposed lock-and-key model

blocks.prompt: 28 The induced fit model was presented by Daniel Koshland in:
blocks.explanation: The American biochemist Daniel Koshland presented the induced fit model in 1958 (Models).

book_ref.quote: an American biochemist Daniel Koshland (1958) presented induced fit model

blocks.prompt: 29 According to the lock-and-key model, the active site is:
blocks.explanation: The lock-and-key model postulates a rigid active site with no modification before, during or after enzyme action (Models).

book_ref.quote: This model postulates that active site is a rigid structure

blocks.prompt: 30 In the induced fit model, binding of the substrate:

options.text: changes the substrate into an inhibitor

blocks.explanation: In the induced fit model, substrate binding induces changes in enzyme structure that let it catalyse more effectively (Models).

book_ref.quote: it induces changes in enzyme structure

blocks.text: 5.4 Factors affecting the rate of enzyme action

blocks.prompt: 31 Enzyme activity is affected by any change that alters the enzyme's:
blocks.explanation: Enzymes are very sensitive to their environment; any change in their chemistry and 3-D shape affects activity (5.4).

book_ref.quote: The activity of an enzyme is affected by any change that alters its chemistry and its three-dimensional shape

blocks.prompt: 32 The optimum temperature for human enzymes is:
blocks.explanation: Every enzyme works fastest at its optimum temperature; for human enzymes it is 37 °C (Temperature).

book_ref.quote: The optimum temperature for human enzymes is 37 °C

blocks.prompt: 33 The shape of an enzyme protein is held by:
blocks.explanation: Hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions hold polypeptide chains in position; slight temperature changes easily disrupt them (Temperature).

book_ref.quote: Both the hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions are easily disrupted by slight changes in temperature

blocks.prompt: 34 Loss of the globular structure of an enzyme at a temperature well above optimum is called:
blocks.explanation: Violent vibrations break bonds holding polypeptide chains, the globular structure is lost: denaturation (Temperature).

book_ref.quote: This phenomenon is known as denaturation of enzyme

blocks.prompt: 35 Below the optimum temperature, the reaction rate is slow because:

options.text: bonds become less flexible and do not permit induced change in the active site

blocks.explanation: Below the optimum, bonds become less flexible and do not permit the induced change in active sites needed for action (Temperature).

book_ref.quote: the bonds that determine enzymes shape become less flexible

blocks.prompt: 36 Thermophilic bacteria of hot springs have enzymes that can function at:
blocks.explanation: Thermophilic bacteria have proteins with stronger bonding and can function at 70 °C or higher (Temperature).

book_ref.quote: can function at temperature of 70 °C or higher

blocks.prompt: 37 A rise in temperature up to a limit increases reaction rate because heat:

options.text: gives kinetic energy so molecules collide more often

blocks.explanation: Heat adds to activation energy and gives kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate move rapidly and collide more frequently (Temperature).

book_ref.quote: Heat also provides kinetic energy to substrate and enzyme molecules

blocks.prompt: 38 Which enzyme shows its optimum activity in an alkaline medium?
blocks.explanation: Pepsin is active in acidic medium (low pH); trypsin shows optimum activity in alkaline medium (high pH) (pH).

book_ref.quote: pepsin is active in acidic medium (low pH) while trypsin shows its optimum activity in alkaline medium

blocks.prompt: 39 An enzyme that works in both acidic and alkaline media is:
blocks.explanation: Papain from green papaya works both in acidic and alkaline media (pH).

book_ref.quote: Some enzymes like papain from green papaya work both in acidic and alkaline media

blocks.prompt: 40 In globular enzymes, pH-sensitive bonds are formed between oppositely charged amino acids such as:
blocks.explanation: Polypeptide chains are held by bonds between oppositely charged amino acids such as glutamic acid (–) and lysine (+), which are sensitive to H⁺ concentration (pH).

book_ref.quote: such as glutamic acid (-) and lysine (+)

blocks.prompt: 41 An extreme change in pH results in:
blocks.explanation: Extreme change in pH can break the bonds in enzymes, resulting in denaturation (pH).

book_ref.quote: Extreme change in pH can break the bonds in enzymes, resulting in enzyme denaturation

blocks.prompt: 42 The optimum pH of pancreatic lipase is:
blocks.explanation: From the table: pancreatic lipase 8.0 (Figure 5.6 corrected: peaks at 1.6 for pepsin and 8 for lipase) (pH).

book_ref.quote: The peaks are drawn at 1.6 and 8 above

blocks.prompt: 43 The optimum pH of pepsin is:
blocks.explanation: Pepsin has optimum pH 1.5–1.6 (book's table; Figure 5.6 corrected) (pH).

book_ref.quote: against the book's own table of optimum pH (pepsin 1.5-1.6, pancreatic lipase 8.0)

blocks.prompt: 44 A change in pH affects enzyme activity mainly by changing:

options.text: the ionization of amino acids at the active site (and of the substrate)

blocks.explanation: A pH change can change ionization of active-site amino acids and may affect the ionization of substrate (pH).

book_ref.quote: Any change in pH can change the ionization of amino acids at active site

blocks.prompt: 45 Enzymes are very efficient because:

options.text: a few enzyme molecules can act on a large amount of substrate

blocks.explanation: A small number of enzyme molecules can catalyse reactions of a large amount of substrate (Enzyme Concentration).

book_ref.quote: a small number of enzyme molecules can catalyse reactions of large amount of substrate

blocks.prompt: 46 With unlimited substrate, increasing enzyme concentration increases the rate because:
blocks.explanation: More enzyme molecules give more active sites, so more substrate is bound and transformed (Enzyme Concentration).

book_ref.quote: When enzyme concentration increases, there are more enzyme molecules and more active sites

blocks.prompt: 47 If enzyme concentration keeps increasing while substrate concentration stays the same, the rate of reaction:
blocks.explanation: With fixed substrate, no more substrate attaches to the extra enzymes, so the rate stays constant (Enzyme Concentration).

book_ref.quote: the rate of reaction stays constant and does not increase further

blocks.prompt: 48 At high substrate concentration the rate of reaction does not increase further because:

options.text: the substrate becomes product without enzyme

blocks.explanation: At high substrate concentration all active sites are occupied; extra substrate finds no free sites (Substrate Concentration).

book_ref.quote: when all active sites of enzymes are occupied (at high substrate concentration)

blocks.prompt: 49 An increase in substrate concentration increases the reaction rate only when:

options.text: enzyme molecules have vacant active sites
an inhibitor blocks the active sites

blocks.explanation: If enzyme molecules have vacant active sites, more substrate increases the rate (Substrate Concentration).

book_ref.quote: If there are enzyme molecules with vacant active sites

blocks.prompt: 50 A chemical that interferes with and blocks an enzyme's activity is called a(n):
blocks.explanation: An inhibitor attaches to an enzyme but is not transformed into products, blocking active sites temporarily or permanently (5.6).

book_ref.quote: A chemical that interferes and blocks an enzyme

blocks.prompt: 51 Aspirin suppresses pain and inflammation by inhibiting the enzymes that produce:
blocks.explanation: Aspirin inhibits enzymes that produce prostaglandin (which causes inflammation) (5.6).

book_ref.quote: It inhibits the enzymes that produce prostaglandin

blocks.prompt: 52 Cyanide blocks cellular respiration by combining with copper and iron in the active site of:
blocks.explanation: Cyanide is an irreversible inhibitor that combines with copper and iron in the active site of cytochrome oxidase (5.6).

book_ref.quote: combines with copper and iron in the active site of enzyme cytochrome oxidase

blocks.prompt: 53 A competitive inhibitor resembles the:
blocks.explanation: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the same binding site (book correction) (Types of Inhibitors).

book_ref.quote: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate, not the enzyme

blocks.prompt: 54 Succinic dehydrogenase oxidizes succinic acid into:
blocks.explanation: Succinic dehydrogenase catalyses the oxidation of succinic acid to fumaric acid (Types of Inhibitors).

book_ref.quote: The enzyme succinic dehydrogenase catalyses the oxidation of succinic acid to fumaric acid

blocks.prompt: 55 Malonic acid inhibits succinic dehydrogenase because it:

options.text: binds at another place and changes the shape
resembles succinic acid and competes for the active site
forms covalent bonds with the enzyme

blocks.explanation: Malonic acid resembles succinic acid, competes for and blocks the active site: competitive inhibition (Types of Inhibitors).

book_ref.quote: Malonic acid has structural similarity with substrate (succinic acid)

blocks.prompt: 56 In the formation of succinyl-CoA by succinyl-CoA synthetase, the product succinyl-CoA acts as a:
blocks.explanation: Succinyl-CoA binds the enzyme as a non-competitive inhibitor, so no more succinyl-CoA is produced (Types of Inhibitors).

book_ref.quote: the product i.e., succinyl CoA acts as a non-competitive inhibitor

blocks.prompt: 57 Irreversible inhibitors bind with the enzyme by:
blocks.explanation: Irreversible inhibitors make covalent bonds; they cannot be released by dilution, dialysis or more substrate (Types of Inhibitors).

book_ref.quote: Irreversible inhibitors make covalent bonds with enzyme

blocks.prompt: 58 Penicillin permanently disables the bacterial enzyme responsible for:
blocks.explanation: Penicillin is an irreversible inhibitor that permanently disables the enzyme building bacterial cell walls (Types of Inhibitors).

book_ref.quote: penicillin permanently disables the enzyme responsible for building bacterial cell walls

blocks.prompt: 59 Malonate is an example of a(n):
blocks.explanation: Reversible inhibitors make weak bonds; malonate temporarily blocks succinate dehydrogenase and the inhibition reverses when it is removed (Types of Inhibitors).

book_ref.quote: Reversible inhibitors make weak bonds (e.g., hydrogen bonds) with enzyme

blocks.prompt: 60 A non-competitive inhibitor:

options.text: binds the enzyme at a place other than the active site

blocks.explanation: A non-competitive inhibitor has no real similarity to substrate, does not enter the active site and binds elsewhere, altering the enzyme's shape (Types of Inhibitors).

book_ref.quote: A non-competitive inhibitor has no real structural similarity to substrate

blocks.prompt: 61 In feedback inhibition, the inhibitor is the:
blocks.explanation: In feedback inhibition the final product reacts with an initial enzyme, changes its conformation and shuts the pathway (Feedback Inhibition).

book_ref.quote: The final product of pathway acts as inhibitor

blocks.prompt: 62 When a cell has more ATP than it needs, ATP:

options.text: inhibits the enzyme that catalyses ATP synthesis

blocks.explanation: Excess ATP acts as a non-competitive inhibitor and blocks the enzyme that catalyses ATP synthesis (Feedback Inhibition).

book_ref.quote: ATP itself acts as a non-competitive inhibitor

blocks.prompt: 63 Inhibitors of enzymes involved in blood clotting are used as:
blocks.explanation: Some inhibitors of blood-clotting enzymes are used as anticoagulants (Significance of Enzyme Inhibition).

book_ref.quote: some inhibitors of enzymes involved in blood clotting are used as anticoagulants

blocks.prompt: 64 Cancer drugs may act by inhibiting enzymes involved in:
blocks.explanation: Many drugs are inhibitors: antibiotics inhibit bacterial enzymes; cancer drugs may inhibit enzymes of cell division (Significance).

book_ref.quote: cancer drugs may inhibit enzymes involved in cell division

blocks.prompt: 65 Enzymes are classified on the basis of:

options.text: the reactions they catalyse and the substrates they use

blocks.explanation: Enzymes are classified on the basis of reactions they catalyse and of substrates they use (5.7).

book_ref.quote: Enzymes are classified on the basis of reactions they catalyse and also on the basis of substrates they use

blocks.prompt: 66 On the basis of the general type of reaction, enzymes are classified into:
blocks.explanation: According to the general type of reaction, enzymes are classified into six classes (Classification on Reactions).

book_ref.quote: enzymes are classified into six classes

blocks.prompt: 67 Hexokinase, which transfers a phosphate group from ATP to glucose, is a(n):
blocks.explanation: Transferases transfer a functional group (methyl, acyl, amino, phosphate) from one substrate to another, e.g. hexokinase (Classification on Reactions).

book_ref.quote: hexokinase transfers phosphate group from ATP to glucose

blocks.prompt: 68 Pyruvate decarboxylase, which removes CO₂ from pyruvic acid, belongs to:
blocks.explanation: Lyases catalyse non-hydrolytic addition or removal of groups such as CO₂ and NH₂, e.g. pyruvate decarboxylase (Classification on Reactions).

book_ref.quote: pyruvate decarboxylase removes CO₂ from pyruvic acid

blocks.prompt: 69 The enzyme class that converts one isomer into another, e.g. glucose into fructose, is:
blocks.explanation: Isomerases catalyse intra-molecular rearrangement; hexose isomerase converts glucose to fructose (Classification on Reactions).

book_ref.quote: hexose isomerase converts glucose to fructose

blocks.prompt: 70 Enzymes that add or remove H⁺ ions or electrons from substrates, such as cytochrome oxidase, are:
blocks.explanation: Oxidoreductases catalyse oxidation/reduction by adding or removing H⁺ ions or electrons, e.g. cytochrome oxidase (Classification on Reactions).

book_ref.quote: cytochrome oxidase catalyses the oxidation of cytochrome

blocks.prompt: 71 Ligases join two molecules by forming new bonds using energy from:
blocks.explanation: Ligases join two molecules by forming new C–C, C–N, C–O or C–S bonds using energy from ATP (Classification on Reactions).

book_ref.quote: two molecules join by forming new C-C, C-N, C-O, or C-S bonds, using energy from ATP

blocks.prompt: 72 Pancreatic lipase hydrolyses lipids into:
blocks.explanation: Lipases act on lipids; pancreatic lipase hydrolyses lipids into fatty acids and glycerol (Classification on Substrates).

book_ref.quote: pancreatic lipase hydrolyses lipids into fatty acids and glycerol

blocks.prompt: 73 The enzyme that breaks dipeptides into amino acids is:
blocks.explanation: Erepsin breaks dipeptides into amino acids (Classification on Substrates).

book_ref.quote: The enzyme that breaks dipeptides into amino acids is erepsin

blocks.prompt: 74 Cellulase breaks cellulose into:
blocks.explanation: Cellulase breaks cellulose into cellobiose (a disaccharide) or glucose (Classification on Substrates).

book_ref.quote: Cellulase breaks cellulose into cellobiose (a disaccharide) or glucose

blocks.prompt: 75 Lactase breaks lactose into:
blocks.explanation: Lactase breaks lactose into glucose and galactose; sucrase gives glucose and fructose; maltase gives glucose (Classification on Substrates).

book_ref.quote: lactase breaks lactose into glucose and galactose

blocks.prompt: 76 Amylase breaks starch or glycogen into:
blocks.explanation: Carbohydrases break bigger carbohydrates into smaller units; amylase breaks starch or glycogen into maltose (Classification on Substrates).

book_ref.quote: amylase acts upon starch or glycogen and breaks them into maltose

blocks.prompt: 77 Pepsin and trypsin break large polypeptides into:
blocks.explanation: Proteases: pepsin and trypsin break large polypeptides into smaller polypeptides (Classification on Substrates).

book_ref.quote: pepsin and trypsin enzymes catalyse the breakdown of large polypeptides into smaller polypeptides

blocks.prompt: 78 Enzymes that act on nucleic acids, such as DNAase and RNAase, are:
blocks.explanation: Nucleases act upon nucleic acids and catalyse their breakdown, e.g. RNAase and DNAase (Classification on Substrates).

book_ref.quote: These enzymes act upon nucleic acids and catalyse their breakdown
